paragraphs: Clustering data with several views means finding groups using different descriptions of the same samples. Missing views make this harder: the available descriptions may give an uneven picture of the data. HA-IMVC addresses both the computational burden of large datasets and the bias that severe incompleteness can introduce into shared representations.

The method uses shared anchors to guide a hypergraph, a structure that represents relationships among groups of samples. This extends the pairwise connections used by conventional anchor graphs, allowing the clustering process to retain higher-order structure. A second component adjusts importance at two levels: it reconciles inconsistent views and reduces the influence of severely incomplete samples on consensus learning.

Experiments across diverse benchmarks report better clustering accuracy while retaining high efficiency, including under severe missingness. The contribution is the combination of richer group relationships with explicit treatment of uneven evidence. Its results support using both structural modeling and adaptive weighting when incomplete observations would otherwise distort the shared clustering structure.
icml-2026-a-consensus-anchor-guided-hype.tldr: HA-IMVC combines group-level relationships and adaptive weighting to improve efficient clustering when many data views are missing.

paragraphs: AURA addresses how a model can recognize affect from images while making its decisions understandable. The paper argues that translating visual evidence into textual descriptions creates a bottleneck: discrete language templates struggle to express continuous emotional variation and can lose subtle visual details. Its alternative is to organize affective understanding around visual archetypes.

These archetypes form a self-organizing representation whose density adapts to affective complexity. In other words, the model allocates more representational detail where the visual distinctions require it. It also breaks affect labels into interpretable visual components arranged in a coherent geometry. This connects predictions to visual resemblance and structure, providing a decision trail grounded in the images themselves.

The paper reports state-of-the-art results on both discrete classification and continuous regression tasks. Those findings support the usefulness of the same visual representation for assigning categories and estimating continuously varying affect. The interpretability contribution is a way to inspect the visual components behind a prediction, alongside the reported improvements in predictive performance.
icml-2026-aura-visually-interpretable-af.tldr: AURA uses adaptive visual archetypes to make affect predictions interpretable while supporting both emotional categories and continuous estimates.

paragraphs: BroRL investigates a different way to spend reinforcement-learning compute after additional training steps begin yielding diminishing returns. It generates hundreds of rollouts for each example, broadening the set of reasoning attempts explored during training. The central question is whether wider exploration can restart improvement in models whose performance has plateaued.

The analysis tracks how reinforcement learning redistributes probability between correct and incorrect tokens. Under a one-step learning assumption, sampled tokens contribute to growth in correct-token probability mass, while unsampled tokens can produce gains or losses. Increasing the rollout count reduces the influence of those unsampled terms, making overall growth more likely. Simulations under relaxed conditions support this account; elimination of knowledge shrinkage is specifically a simulator finding.

Empirically, BroRL improves models saturated after 3,000 ProRL steps and produces continued gains for a 1.5-billion-parameter model. Under equal training time, it also reports better data and compute efficiency. Generation throughput nearly doubles in the authors’ hardware setup, alongside fewer filtered samples during dynamic sampling. These results support exploration breadth as a complementary scaling direction.
icml-2026-brorl-scaling-reinforcement-le.tldr: BroRL broadens reinforcement-learning exploration with hundreds of rollouts per example, sustaining empirical gains after longer training has plateaued.

paragraphs: This paper studies private estimation of cumulative distributions across categories when some numerical responses are more sensitive than others. A category may seem harmless by itself yet become identifying when paired with a sensitive value. The proposed mechanism handles this interaction by selectively withholding identifying details when a response could reveal sensitive content.

The mechanism operates within utility-optimized local differential privacy, allowing protection to reflect unequal sensitivity across responses. Its censoring provides plausible deniability without requiring an exact sensitive region to be specified in advance. That flexibility matters when privacy concerns cannot be captured by a fixed boundary. The method can also be used with symmetric local differential privacy, where censoring still reduces the need for perturbation.

The authors establish uniform consistency and pointwise weak convergence results, providing theoretical support for the resulting estimates and their limiting statistical behavior. Numerical experiments on synthetic and real data further support the methodology. The contribution joins a more adaptable privacy mechanism with statistical guarantees for distribution estimation, while accounting for the identifying potential of accompanying categories.
icml-2026-censoring-with-plausible-denia.tldr: The paper introduces selective censoring for private distribution estimation when numerical values and accompanying categories carry unequal privacy risks.

paragraphs: Video diffusion transformers spend substantial computation on attention across space and time. Sparse attention reduces that cost by keeping selected interactions, but coarse blocks can miss important fine-grained patterns. DFSAttn addresses the fact that these patterns also change dynamically, making aggressive sparsification especially prone to reducing generation quality.

The authors first derive a lower bound on attention recall to identify factors that govern block sparsity’s effectiveness. Their training-free framework then combines three mechanisms. Hilbert-curve token reordering supports finer selection while retaining efficient GPU execution. Hierarchical scoring estimates which blocks matter, and cached sparse masks with adaptive ratios balance accuracy against computational savings. Together, these choices connect the structure of attention selection to practical execution efficiency.

Experiments report consistently stronger results than prior methods at high sparsity, with up to 2.1 times end-to-end speedup while maintaining high generation quality. This is a measured maximum rather than a uniform acceleration guarantee. The findings indicate that carefully arranging and selecting attention blocks can make substantial sparsity useful without requiring model retraining.
icml-2026-dfsattn-dynamic-fine-grained-s.tldr: DFSAttn dynamically selects fine-grained attention blocks, achieving up to 2.1 times faster video generation while maintaining high quality.

paragraphs: Speculative reasoning accelerates multimodal reasoning by proposing draft steps that a target model verifies. Its usefulness depends on how well those drafts match the target’s reasoning: misaligned proposals can waste work or introduce errors. DREAM-R coordinates draft training, verification, and execution to make more of this speculative work useful.

Its reinforcement-learning objective, SAPO, trains the draft model to produce concise steps that remain faithful to target reasoning trajectories. A threshold-based verifier then uses a ratio criterion to accept steps only when positive evidence clearly dominates. The execution framework runs drafting, target reasoning, and verification in parallel across multiple steps, with support for early stopping and fallback when speculative progress cannot be used.

On reasoning-heavy benchmarks, DREAM-R reports up to 2.49 times speedup while preserving target-model accuracy. The result links efficiency to three complementary choices: better-aligned drafts, selective acceptance, and overlapping computation. It demonstrates that speculative reasoning can deliver substantial measured acceleration when these components work together, with the reported accuracy preservation applying to the evaluated tasks.
icml-2026-dream-r-multimodal-speculative.tldr: DREAM-R combines aligned drafts, selective verification, and parallel execution for up to 2.49 times faster multimodal reasoning at preserved target accuracy.

paragraphs: Long videos create large key-value caches in multimodal language models, making memory a major obstacle to processing extended sequences. Existing compression approaches can break temporal continuity or assign the same memory budget to every layer. EAKV starts from the observation that layers differ in how much semantic information they contain.

The framework uses attention entropy to guide adaptive allocation of cache space without additional training. It preserves critical tokens and condenses redundant context into compact contextual anchors. This gives compression two roles: deciding where memory is most valuable and retaining a compact representation of information that would otherwise be discarded. The allocation is intended to track semantic density across layers.

Experiments across multiple benchmarks, architectures, and model sizes report improvements ranging from 0.6% to 6.5% over existing methods. These findings support adapting compression to the model’s internal information distribution. The contribution is a memory-allocation strategy that combines selective retention with contextual summarization, addressing both uneven layer requirements and the continuity needed for understanding long videos.
icml-2026-eakv-an-entropy-driven-adaptiv.tldr: EAKV uses attention entropy to allocate cache memory across layers while preserving important video tokens and compact contextual anchors.

paragraphs: Clinical prediction models can lose accuracy when the electronic health records encountered during deployment differ from their training data. Domain adaptation can help, but an opaque adaptation process makes predictions difficult to inspect. ExtraCare aims to improve prediction under distribution shifts while exposing how its internal representation relates to medical concepts.

The model separates patient representations into invariant and covariant components, distinguishing shared information from variation associated with the domain. Both components receive supervision, and training enforces orthogonality between them. This arrangement is intended to preserve information relevant to prediction while explicitly representing domain differences. For explanations, sparse latent dimensions are mapped to medical concepts, and targeted ablations measure their contributions to model predictions.

Evaluation on two real-world health-record datasets, using several domain partitions, reports strong predictive performance and improved transparency. Extensive case studies provide evidence for the explanations. The findings support treating domain variation as something to expose and structure, alongside learning transferable information, so that adaptation produces both useful predictions and inspectable accounts of their contributing concepts.
icml-2026-exploring-accurate-and-transpa.tldr: ExtraCare separates shared and domain-varying patient information and connects predictions to medical concepts for more transparent healthcare adaptation.

paragraphs: Converting an autoregressive language model into a diffusion model changes both the data it sees during post-training and the attention pattern it uses. The paper identifies this mismatch as a source of limited speed gains or degraded performance. Jacobi Forcing instead post-trains the original model to predict multiple tokens while retaining causal attention.

Training uses the model’s own parallel-generation trajectories from Jacobi decoding. A progressive distillation procedure teaches it to advance farther along those trajectories in each step. This makes parallel prediction part of the learned behavior while staying closer to the model’s original causal setup. A further decoding method processes multiple blocks and recycles rejected work to increase the number of accepted tokens per iteration.

The trained models achieve 3.8 times wall-clock speedup on coding and mathematics benchmarks with minimal performance loss. Multi-block decoding with rejection recycling reaches up to 4.6 times the token acceptance count per iteration and 4.0 times wall-clock speedup. The latter explicitly trades additional computation for reduced latency, distinguishing faster completion from simply doing less computational work.
icml-2026-fast-and-accurate-causal-paral.tldr: Jacobi Forcing trains causal language models for parallel token prediction, reaching up to 4.0 times wall-clock speedup with an enhanced decoder.

paragraphs: Vision-language-action models must translate visual observations and instructions into robot behavior, but their performance can degrade when environments change. BehaviorVLA addresses representations that fragment behavior into short intervals or align execution too rigidly. It aims to capture a coherent behavior over longer trajectories and adapt its realization to the task’s current progress.

The framework pairs a behavior encoder with a phase-conditioned decoder. The encoder uses a causal Mamba-based architecture to combine long-horizon trajectory information into a unified representation. The decoder turns that representation into actions while dynamically aligning task-level prior information with real-time execution progress. This connects an abstract account of the behavior with the changing requirements of carrying it out.

Reported results include 58% on RoboTwin 2.0, 98% on LIBERO, and 4.36 average length on CALVIN, described as state-of-the-art outcomes. In real-world simulation-to-reality transfer, BehaviorVLA matches OpenVLA-OFT using half the demonstration data. These findings support the value of temporal coherence and progress-aware decoding for both task performance and data efficiency in the evaluated settings.
icml-2026-from-abstraction-to-instantiat.tldr: BehaviorVLA combines long-horizon behavior encoding with progress-aware action decoding to improve robotic manipulation and demonstration efficiency.

paragraphs: Multi-view clustering combines different descriptions of the same data to discover shared groups. Anchor-based methods reduce computation by using representative points, but static anchors at a single level can miss structure at different granularities. HAG-MVC organizes the data into a hierarchy so that fine distinctions and broader groupings can be represented together.

Its pyramid contains multiple levels of anchors and graph structure. These are refined jointly through repeated updates, allowing the representatives and their connections to evolve together from fine to coarse scales. All anchors stay within the original feature space. This gives users a way to inspect the abstraction process through the anchors themselves, rather than relying solely on inaccessible internal representations.

Experiments on benchmark datasets report consistent improvements over state-of-the-art methods. The results support hierarchical refinement as a useful extension of efficient anchor-based clustering. The paper also presents the architecture as a broader approach to hierarchical knowledge representation; the concrete empirical findings described in the abstract concern multi-view clustering and the benefits of its inspectable, multilevel structure.
icml-2026-hierarchical-anchor-graph-lear.tldr: HAG-MVC jointly refines anchors and graphs across multiple levels to improve multi-view clustering while keeping its abstractions inspectable.

paragraphs: Block-wise diffusion language models can generate multiple tokens in parallel, but pushing parallelism too aggressively often reduces accuracy. LightningRL treats the balance between correct answers and tokens generated per forward pass as a post-training objective. Its premise is that a model can learn useful, highly parallel generation trajectories without making every trajectory equally aggressive.

The method builds on Group Relative Policy Optimization with rewards for both final accuracy and inference parallelism. It normalizes these rewards separately to stabilize training, adds a token-level likelihood loss on correct trajectories, and uses dynamic sampling with filtering informed by tokens per forward pass. These components jointly encourage efficient generation while reinforcing successful reasoning paths.

Across mathematics and coding tasks, the reported results improve the frontier of achievable accuracy and parallelism. LightningRL maintains competitive accuracy while reaching an average of 7.3 tokens per forward pass, with up to 11.10 on MBPP. These are parallelism measurements, so the contribution is specifically a better demonstrated quality–parallelism balance through reinforcement learning.
icml-2026-lightningrl-breaking-the-accur.tldr: LightningRL rewards correctness and parallel generation together, improving the accuracy–parallelism frontier of block-wise diffusion language models.

paragraphs: MoVie brings semantic guidance into video compression, addressing codecs that concentrate on low-level motion and can lose perceptual quality in complex scenes. Its central processing block combines transformer and convolutional components, using windows to model local spatial structure and temporal dynamics. Text provides an additional source of semantic information.

An Extractor and an Injector incorporate text through two stages of fusion. History-conditioned coding draws on both previous frames and aggregated historical frames to reduce redundancy and support temporal coherence. A spatial–channel factorized entropy model estimates probabilities using spatial neighborhoods and channel groups, helping allocate bits adaptively. These designs work together to improve reconstruction at low bitrates.

On UVG and MCL-JCV, MoVie reports BD-rate changes of −50.23% for FID and −14.64% for LPIPS using VGGNet, relative to HM. Its per-pixel computation is 55.76% of DCVC-FM’s kMACs. These comparisons concern different reference methods and measures. A human study also reports consistent preference over strong baselines, supporting the claimed perceptual benefits alongside the measured rate and computation results.
icml-2026-movie-multimodal-video-compres.tldr: MoVie combines text guidance, temporal history, and adaptive bit allocation to improve the perceptual efficiency of video compression.

paragraphs: Updating a Cox survival model online is difficult because its usual partial likelihood couples observations through risk sets. Each update can require information spanning the dataset, undermining the goal of processing incoming data without retaining historical records. COLSA changes the statistical formulation to make these updates manageable.

The framework replaces partial likelihood with a full likelihood that approximates the baseline hazard using a sieve representation. The resulting objective decomposes across observations, enabling updates without storing historical data. COLSA maintains sufficient statistics for a higher-order basis and projects that basis according to the data, adapting model complexity to the effective sample size while using constant memory.

The authors establish asymptotic normality and the same statistical efficiency as the pooled-data partial likelihood estimator. These are large-sample guarantees, connecting streaming estimation to a standard full-data reference. Simulations and an application to kidney transplant data report better performance than existing online methods and results matching full-data estimation. Together, the theory and experiments support online survival analysis that retains strong inferential properties without repeated access to all observations.
icml-2026-online-learning-and-inference-.tldr: COLSA enables constant-memory online Cox estimation with asymptotic statistical efficiency matching pooled-data partial likelihood estimation.

paragraphs: Reasoning models that retrieve information need feedback about which retrieval steps actually help. Final-answer correctness alone provides limited guidance about intermediate searches. InfoReasoner introduces a denser training signal based on how much retrieved information reduces uncertainty in the model’s beliefs, while keeping that signal connected to answer correctness.

The theoretical formulation establishes non-negativity, additivity across successive steps, and channel monotonicity for this notion of information gain. The practical implementation estimates semantic uncertainty from the model’s output distributions. It groups outputs using bidirectional textual entailment, so mutually supporting meanings inform the reward. This supplies credit for individual retrieval steps without requiring people to annotate those intermediate actions.

The framework trains with Group Relative Policy Optimization and reports consistent improvements over strong retrieval-augmented baselines on seven question-answering benchmarks, MATH500, and WebDetective. These findings support semantic information gain as a useful optimization signal for information seeking. The contribution connects a principled account of uncertainty reduction to a scalable reward that can guide the retrieval process throughout reasoning.
icml-2026-optimizing-agentic-reasoning-w.tldr: InfoReasoner rewards retrieval steps for reducing semantic uncertainty while anchoring training to final-answer correctness.

paragraphs: Privacy-aware language-model agents face a computational trade-off: direct generation is fast, while explicit reasoning about whether information sharing fits its context adds overhead. PrivGate uses signals inside the model to decide when that extra reasoning is warranted. It aims to concentrate privacy-related computation on situations that appear risky.

The framework builds on the finding that privacy sensitivity is linearly represented in the model’s residual stream, including during generation that violates contextual privacy requirements. Its latent gate reads this internal structure and triggers explicit reasoning when detected risk is high. The gating mechanism requires no fine-tuning of the base model, making selective intervention possible without retraining the underlying generator.

On PrivacyLens, PrivGate reports consistently strong identification of risks outside the distribution used to establish the detector. End-to-end evaluations show a 62.6% average relative reduction in privacy leakage with 15.9% token overhead. The results demonstrate a measured improvement in the privacy–efficiency balance: internal risk signals can help target additional reasoning where it is useful, while leakage is reduced rather than reported as eliminated.
icml-2026-privgate-steering-contextual-i.tldr: PrivGate uses internal privacy signals to trigger reasoning selectively, reducing average privacy leakage by 62.6% relative with 15.9% token overhead.

paragraphs: Retrieval systems often improve a difficult query by expanding it or searching repeatedly, then discard those adaptations. Evolving Retrieval Memory preserves useful gains by updating document keys in the retrieval index. The aim is to let previous successful searches improve future retrieval without repeatedly paying for query-time adaptation.

ERM uses correctness-gated feedback to decide which changes are worth retaining. It attributes individual expansion signals to the document keys they benefit, then updates those keys with stable, norm-bounded steps. This selective process addresses the semantic drift and accumulated noise associated with less disciplined index updates. The framework operates without model training.

The authors show that query expansion and key expansion are theoretically equivalent under standard similarity functions and prove convergence of ERM’s selective updates. Experiments on BEIR and BRIGHT across 13 domains report consistent retrieval and generation gains, especially on reasoning-intensive tasks. The stated zero inference-time overhead concerns using the evolved index at native retrieval speed: useful adaptation is accumulated in persistent retrieval representations rather than recomputed for every query.
icml-2026-rag-without-forgetting-continu.tldr: ERM turns successful query expansions into stable document-key updates, improving subsequent retrieval without added inference-time overhead.

paragraphs: Referring video segmentation usually assumes that the object described by a user is already visible. RVAS extends the problem to cases where the system must first explore to find it. Success therefore requires deciding how to search, locating the referred object, and segmenting it once the relevant view is obtained.

The authors introduce a large dataset with manually annotated exploration actions and reference reasoning traces to support supervised training and evaluation. Their benchmark shows that representative segmentation and related video-understanding methods struggle with active search, while adding online decisions creates substantial overhead. This establishes exploration as a distinct capability that existing passive perception systems do not readily provide.

The proposed LESA baseline combines a state controller and hierarchical memory for streaming processing, invoking multimodal language-model reasoning sparsely. It substantially reduces inference cost while retaining competitive planning quality and consistently improving segmentation accuracy on the RVAS dataset. The paper contributes both an evaluation setting for finding initially unseen targets and a framework that coordinates search and segmentation efficiently.
icml-2026-rvas-referring-video-active-ex.tldr: RVAS introduces active search before video-object segmentation, with a dataset and an efficient memory-based baseline called LESA.

paragraphs: Information-extraction systems often assume that a schema defining relevant types and relationships already exists. SCOPE evaluates the upstream task of constructing that schema from text. It draws on 24 public extraction sources, using training text for induction and reserving normalized gold schema graphs for evaluation.

SCION is an auditable reference pipeline that builds candidate schemas from the text. Naming, merging, filtering, validation, and optional conservative fusion must remain tied to candidate-linked evidence and strict JSON contracts. The benchmark’s core event target includes event types and argument roles within events, with links between events evaluated separately. This makes the intended output and the evidence supporting construction decisions explicit.

SCION-lite achieves the highest F1 among the compared approaches across four schema-graph metric families on the core suite. A compact open-model variant reduces reliance on proprietary models. These results measure agreement with normalized typed-edge targets; they do not establish superiority over human ontology design. Released evidence-linked outputs and processing logs make the pipeline’s decisions and failures available for inspection.
icml-2026-scope-and-scion-a-benchmark-an.tldr: SCOPE benchmarks schema construction from text, while SCION provides an evidence-linked pipeline with strong measured schema-graph performance.

paragraphs: EEG emotion-recognition models can classify accurately while leaving the meaning of their internal features difficult to understand. This paper makes those representations more accessible by translating EEG signals into identity-anonymized facial emojis. It treats explanation as cross-modal generation, giving an observable behavioral form to the model’s representation of emotional change.

The framework combines FMENet, which models spatial relationships relevant to expression, with a Facial Emoji Learning Branch. Reconstructing emojis acts as a structured semantic regularizer: the learned EEG representation must support meaningful facial dynamics as well as emotion recognition. The design draws inspiration from associations between neural activity and facial behavior, using animated expressions as an interpretable proxy.

Experiments on EAV and MMER report state-of-the-art accuracy among models using EEG alone. The generated facial animations are described as semantically faithful and provide a visual account of emotional evolution without reproducing personal identity. The findings support combining recognition with an interpretable generation task, so the same framework produces both emotion predictions and a privacy-preserving visual representation of the signals.
icml-2026-see-the-emotion-a-facial-emoji.tldr: The framework translates EEG into anonymized facial animations, pairing interpretable emotional visualization with strong EEG-only recognition accuracy.

paragraphs: Long reasoning traces can contain redundant work, but shortening them indiscriminately can remove steps needed for a correct answer. SmartThinker addresses this tension during reinforcement learning. It replaces a static preference for shorter responses with a progressively adjusted length target that reflects the relationship between response length and accuracy during training.

The method uses Group Relative Policy Optimization and dynamically estimates the response length associated with peak accuracy. It then encourages overlong responses to move toward that estimate. A second adjustment changes the strength of the length reward, helping avoid unjustified penalties on correct reasoning paths. These two controls adapt both the target length and the pressure applied to reach it.

Experiments report up to 52.6% length compression with improved accuracy, as well as up to 16.6% relative accuracy improvement on challenging benchmarks such as AIME25. These are reported maxima, not a fixed outcome for every problem. The findings support calibrating reasoning length from training behavior so that efficiency gains can coexist with stronger task performance.
icml-2026-smartthinker-progressive-chain.tldr: SmartThinker adaptively calibrates reasoning length and reward strength, reporting up to 52.6% shorter reasoning with improved accuracy.

paragraphs: Removing selected training data’s influence becomes more complicated when a model has learned through a sequence of tasks. Earlier updates affect later ones, so unlearning must account for accumulated model evolution. This paper develops a theoretical framework connecting certified unlearning with continual learning and the need to retain useful historical knowledge.

The authors express post-unlearning excess risk as a combination of continual-learning excess risk and unlearning loss. This separates errors associated with sequential learning from the cost of targeted forgetting. Under assumptions described as mild, they establish an upper bound for continual-learning excess risk in non-convex models, then adapt gradient-based and Hessian-based certified unlearning approaches to this setting.

Their analysis finds that the gradient-based approach is less effective at minimizing unlearning loss but requires nearly zero storage overhead to enable unlearning. The Hessian-based approach offers a different performance–storage balance. This motivates a hybrid method that reduces storage costs while maintaining post-unlearning performance. Experiments support the theoretical findings, making storage requirements an explicit part of the forgetting–retention trade-off.
icml-2026-the-forgetting-retention-dilem.tldr: The paper formalizes unlearning in continual learning and develops a hybrid approach balancing targeted forgetting, retained performance, and storage cost.

paragraphs: A model learning successive tasks can accumulate damage from poisoned data, potentially diverging or suffering large prediction errors. This paper analyzes attacks and defenses specifically for regularization-based continual learning. It models the interaction as an online zero-sum game, giving a formal setting for asking when successful defense is possible.

The first result establishes an impossibility boundary: no defense succeeds in this setting when an adversary poisons a linear proportion of tasks with unbounded noise or pattern shifts. The authors then examine two more restricted regimes that may admit defenses. These separate limited attack frequency from limited attack magnitude, clarifying which constraint makes a proposed defense relevant.

For infrequent attacks, a task-to-task verification mechanism detects poisoning and reduces accumulated bias to support convergence. For bounded noise per attack, a robust defense reduces sensitivity to poisoned features and provably accelerates convergence. Experiments on realistic tasks support the theory. The contribution pairs a sharply qualified impossibility result with defenses designed for particular attack conditions, rather than claiming protection against unrestricted poisoning.
icml-2026-theory-of-continual-learning-a.tldr: The paper establishes poisoning limits for regularization-based continual learning and develops defenses for infrequent attacks or bounded attack noise.

paragraphs: Vision-language navigation agents encounter environments whose properties change over time. Updating separately for each new environment can discard useful knowledge or transfer unsuitable knowledge from previous settings. IDEA treats adaptation results as reusable assets, allowing experience from earlier domains to contribute to later navigation.

The framework optimizes soft prompts using Fisher-guided weighting to capture transferable information. It stores these prompts together with domain coordinates in a growing library. For a new target domain, it constructs a bridge by projecting the target onto the convex hull of historical knowledge. This uses combinations of stored assets to provide a better initialization for subsequent prompt optimization.

The library and bridge reinforce one another: accumulated prompts improve initialization, and newly optimized prompts expand the available assets. Experiments on REVERIE, R2R, and R2R-CE report consistent superiority over existing methods. The paper also reports training-free adaptation through asset sharing, alongside its prompt-optimization procedure. The broader finding is that retaining and composing adaptation results can make online adjustment more useful across changing environments.
icml-2026-turning-adaptation-into-assets.tldr: IDEA stores and combines domain-specific prompts so navigation agents can reuse earlier adaptations when environments change.

paragraphs: This paper asks how much expressive power softmax attention has on its own when paired with linear transformations. It proves that two self-attention layers, or one self-attention layer followed by a softmax function, can universally approximate continuous sequence-to-sequence functions on compact domains. These are sufficient architectural constructions under the stated function and domain conditions.

The proof introduces an interpolation-based way to analyze attention’s internal operation. Its key step shows that self-attention can approximate a generalized ReLU function to arbitrary precision. This connects attention to mechanisms already known to support universal approximation. The authors also establish corresponding sufficient constructions using multi-head attention, extending the analysis to that architecture.

Earlier transformer approximation results relied on feed-forward networks, so the contribution identifies expressive capacity within attention itself. The same techniques show that attention-only layers, with the relevant softmax construction, can approximate gradient descent performed in context. These are representational results: they establish what the architectures can approximate, including an optimization procedure, rather than an empirical claim about how reliably training discovers those computations.
icml-2026-universal-approximation-with-s.tldr: The paper proves that small softmax-attention constructions with linear transformations universally approximate continuous sequence functions on compact domains.
